udl.lead: Practical ways to open the K–8 Science Critical Thinking Online Breakouts to every learner, organized by the three principles of the CAST Universal Design for Learning Guidelines (version 3.0). Every breakout — featured and concept — already builds in many of these supports across all seven languages.

elps.lead: How to use the K–8 Science breakouts with emergent bilingual students, aligned to the Texas English Language Proficiency Standards across listening, speaking, reading, and writing.

guide.lead: A ready structure for building a science lesson around a Critical Thinking Online Breakout, following a standard Texas lesson-plan format. A worked Grade 6 example appears at the end.
guide.ex.name: Grade 6 · States of Matter
guide.ex.bigidea: Matter exists in states whose particle arrangement and motion explain their properties.
guide.ex.eq: How does the arrangement of particles explain whether matter is a solid, liquid, or gas?
guide.ex.obj: Students will compare the particle arrangement and behavior of solids, liquids, and gases and use it to explain a property.
guide.ex.vocab: particle, state of matter, solid, liquid, gas

elps.lead: How to use the Bible as Literature breakouts with emergent bilingual students, aligned to the Texas English Language Proficiency Standards across listening, speaking, reading, and writing.

guide.lead: A ready structure for building a literary-analysis lesson around a Critical Thinking Online Breakout, following a standard Texas lesson-plan format. A worked example appears at the end.
guide.ex.name: The Parable of the Prodigal Son (structure & theme)
guide.ex.bigidea: A parable uses a simple story structure to carry a larger moral or theme.
guide.ex.eq: How does the structure of a parable shape the lesson a reader takes from it?
guide.ex.obj: Students will identify the structure of a parable and explain the theme it develops, citing textual evidence.
guide.ex.vocab: parable, theme, structure, moral, figurative language

udl.lead: Practical ways to open the CLEAR Critical Thinking Breakouts to every learner, organized by the three principles of the CAST Universal Design for Learning Guidelines (version 3.0). Each activity walks the CLEAR process — Claim, Lens, Evidence, Alternatives, Response — and already builds in many of these supports across all seven languages.

elps.lead: How to use the CLEAR Critical Thinking Breakouts with emergent bilingual students, aligned to the Texas English Language Proficiency Standards across listening, speaking, reading, and writing.

guide.lead: A ready structure for building a critical-thinking lesson around a breakout using the CLEAR process, following a standard Texas lesson-plan format. A worked example appears at the end.
guide.ex.name: Evaluating a Claim with the CLEAR Process
guide.ex.bigidea: Strong thinking tests a claim against evidence and alternatives before responding.
guide.ex.eq: How do we decide whether a claim is well supported?
guide.ex.obj: Students will evaluate a claim by weighing evidence and considering at least one alternative before responding.

guide.ex.name: Reading the Declaration of Independence
guide.ex.bigidea: The Declaration of Independence states a claim and the reasons a people may govern themselves.
guide.ex.eq: What claim does the Declaration make, and what evidence supports it?
guide.ex.obj: Students will identify the central claim of the Declaration and two supporting reasons, citing the text.

guide.ex.name: Frederick Douglass — “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?”
guide.ex.bigidea: Freedom's meaning depends on who is asking; Douglass exposes the gap between a nation's ideals and its reality.
guide.ex.eq: How does Douglass use the Fourth of July to challenge his audience?
guide.ex.obj: Students will explain the central argument of Douglass's speech and identify two pieces of evidence he uses.

common.footer: Idioms & Sayings for Multilingual Learners · Runs in your browser — no logins, no data collected.

udl.lead: Practical ways to open the Idioms & Sayings for Multilingual Learners breakouts (Grades 3–12) to every learner, organized by the three principles of the CAST Universal Design for Learning Guidelines (version 3.0). Each breakout separates the literal picture from the real meaning and compares the idiom across languages — welcoming the home language as a resource — and already builds in many of these supports across all seven languages.

elps.lead: How to use the Idioms & Sayings breakouts (Grades 3–12) with emergent bilingual students, aligned to the Texas English Language Proficiency Standards across listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Idiomatic and figurative language is named directly in the ELPS, and each learner's home language is treated as an asset for decoding it.

guide.lead: A ready structure for building a figurative-language lesson around a Critical Thinking Online Breakout, following a standard Texas lesson-plan format. A worked example appears at the end.
guide.ex.name: Grades 3–5 · Body Idioms (literal picture vs. real meaning)
guide.ex.bigidea: An idiom's meaning is not the sum of its words; readers use context and cross-linguistic comparison to find the real meaning.
guide.ex.eq: How do strong readers figure out what an idiom really means?
guide.ex.obj: Students will distinguish the literal picture from the figurative meaning of an idiom and compare it to an equivalent saying in their home language.
guide.ex.lang: Students explain — in English or their home language — what an idiom means and name an equivalent saying from their L1 (translanguaging).
guide.ex.vocab: idiom, figurative language, literal, context, home language (L1)
